transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I... I guess I'm here because things have just gotten so dark lately, you know? Like, really dark. I wake up—when I actually can sleep, which isn't often—and my first thought is just, 'Why did I wake up?' It just feels like it would be so much better, so much easier for everyone, if I just... didn't. If I just went to sleep and that was it. And it's not just a passing thought, it's like this heavy blanket over me all day while I'm trying to work. I lay carpet and tile, you know, and it's hard work, on your knees all day, and lately, I just stare at the floor and think about how dying would just be... fair. Like a fair punishment. Because I've just ruined everything. I've let my family down, I've messed things up with my crew at work... I just feel like I'm a burden, and maybe if I was gone, they wouldn't have to deal with me anymore. I just can't shake this feeling that I deserve to die for all the mistakes I've made, and it just plays over and over in my head.
Have you ever felt this way for a period of at least two weeks at any point in your life before this current stretch?

I... I don't really know. I mean, I guess it's possible? It's just so hard to remember what things were like before this, you know? Like, when you're in the middle of it, when it's this heavy, it feels like it's always been this way. I try to think back to, like, a year ago, or five years ago, and it's all just a blur of laying tile, driving to the next job, coming home... I know there were times I felt down, sure. Everyone feels down sometimes, especially when the work dries up or when my knees are just screaming at me after a twelve-hour day on the floor. But this... this feeling of just wanting to disappear, of feeling like I *should* disappear because I'm so worthless... I don't know if I've ever felt it this strongly, or for this long, before right now. Or maybe I did and I just pushed it down? I used to be so good at just putting my head down and working through things. You know, just spread the mortar, lay the tile, make sure the lines are straight, and don't think about anything else. But now I can't even do that. The thoughts just bleed into everything. So, to answer your question... I honestly couldn't tell you if it's ever been exactly two weeks like this before. It just feels like forever right now.
Looking back over your life, can you recall any specific periods, perhaps lasting a few months, where you felt this same heavy, hopeless way, even if you managed to push through it at the time?

Well... okay, if I really sit and try to trace it back... yeah. Yeah, I can pinpoint it, actually. It hasn't just been a few months. It’s been... gosh, it’s been about a year and two months now. I know that because it started a little bit after my husband’s injury. He got hurt at his job, and it was this whole big thing with worker's comp and him being laid up, and I had to take on extra shifts. I was doing all the heavy lifting, literally, at work, carrying rolls of carpet up three flights of stairs by myself because my partner called out, and then coming home to try and take care of him. And at first, you know, I thought I was just exhausted. Like, bone-tired from the physical labor and the stress of the bills piling up on the kitchen counter. I remember sitting at the table, looking at the electric bill, and just crying, which isn't like me. I’m the one who fixes things. I lay the floor, I make a solid foundation, you know? But then... it just never lifted. Even when he started physical therapy and things got a tiny bit easier at home, this... this darkness just stayed. It settled in right around then, about fourteen months ago, and it’s just been this constant, heavy weight pulling me down every single day since. I kept thinking, 'Okay, next week I'll feel better, next week I'll have energy,' but it just kept stretching on and on, month after month, until here we are, over a year later, and I just can't see the light anymore.

During these past fourteen months, have there been any periods of at least two weeks where you felt so slowed down that other people might have noticed you moving or speaking much more sluggishly than usual, or conversely, felt so agitated that you couldn't sit still?

Well, I... I don't think so? I mean, I'm always tired, like I said, bone-tired. When you're hauling boxes of ceramic tile out of a van and mixing thinset all day, you're not exactly moving like a ballerina when you get home, you know? My knees ache, my back aches, and sometimes it takes me a minute just to stand up straight after I've been kneeling for hours. So, yeah, I guess I move slow, but that's just the job. That's the physical toll of it. I've never had anyone at work pull me aside and say, 'Hey, you're moving like molasses today,' or anything like that. My crew, they know I work hard. I've always been a hard worker. Even with this... this heavy blanket over me, I still try to keep up the pace. And as for being agitated or not being able to sit still... no, not really. If anything, all I want to do is sit still. Or lay down. I just want to lay down and not have to move or think or do anything at all. When I get home, I just kind of collapse on the couch, and my husband—bless him, he tries—he'll ask me about my day, and I just... I don't even have the energy to talk. I just kind of stare at the TV without really watching it. So, no, no pacing around or feeling like I have a motor running inside me. It's more like the motor just completely died, and I'm just this heavy, empty shell trying to drag myself through the day. I don't think anyone would say I'm moving unusually slow for what I do, just... normal tired from the work, even if inside it feels like I'm walking through wet concrete.
